paragraphs.heading: One-way time
paragraphs.text: The arrow of time is the idea that time runs in one direction only, so it is not symmetric. The British astrophysicist Arthur Eddington developed it in 1927, and it is still an unsolved question in physics. Eddington thought the direction could be found by studying how atoms, molecules and larger bodies are organized.

paragraphs.heading: The puzzle
paragraphs.text: The puzzle was first noticed in the 1800s in the study of gases and other substances. At the microscopic level, physical laws are thought to hold just as well, or almost as well, if time runs backwards. At the everyday scale, though, time plainly flows one way. A simple test: if time were perfectly symmetric, a video of real events would look believable played either forwards or backwards.

paragraphs.heading: A ball shows the difference
paragraphs.text: Gravity works the same in both directions of time. A ball thrown up, slowing, stopping and falling would look just as real on film run in reverse. But a ball that bounces and gradually comes to rest cannot be run backwards believably. As it goes forward, its energy of motion is lost and its entropy, which can be pictured as a gauge of disorder at the tiny scale, rises. Entropy may be one of the few processes that cannot be reversed in time.

paragraphs.heading: Finding the direction
paragraphs.text: There is a simple rule for finding the arrow's direction. Draw an arrow any way you like: if following it brings more and more randomness into the world, it points to the future, and if randomness shrinks, it points to the past. On this view, that is the only difference between the two that physics knows, since bringing in randomness is the one thing that cannot be undone. This one-way property has no match in space, and it shows up in science only when many individuals are organized together.

paragraphs.heading: The second law
paragraphs.text: The thermodynamic arrow of time comes from the second law of thermodynamics, which says entropy tends to grow over time in an isolated system. So as time passes, such a system becomes more disordered in a statistical sense. This lets us tell the future from the past, although measuring entropy does not measure time accurately. In an open system, entropy can even go down.

paragraphs.heading: Near the Big Bang
paragraphs.text: In his book The Big Picture, the physicist Sean Carroll compares time with space. Physical laws treat all directions in space alike, yet near Earth up and down are clearly different, because a huge body is close by. In the same way, the laws mostly do not care which way time runs, but we are relatively close in time to the Big Bang, and that special event breaks the symmetry. On this view, every arrow of time comes from our nearness to the Big Bang and the special conditions it had.

paragraphs.heading: Memory and language
paragraphs.text: There is also a mental arrow: we sense ourselves moving from a known past toward an unknown future. We remember the past but not the future, and we feel we can affect the future but not the past. Languages place time in space in different ways. English puts the past behind and the future ahead, but that is a cultural habit: the Aymara language puts the past ahead and the future behind, matching a past that has been seen and a future that has not.
